content: 1. Individuals who receive condoms without also receiving lubricant are excluded from this count. 2. If data specific to key populations are available from mainstream programs, they can also be included in this indicator. 3. To prevent double counting, methods such as unique identifier codes or the recall last contact method can be employed. 4. Different time periods can be selected when measuring this indicator, as varying durations provide distinct insights into program reach and service utilization frequency. 5. For instance, reporting on access within the last month offers a snapshot of current utilization and approximates the number of individuals who may regularly use the service. 6. If population size estimates are unavailable, monitoring changes in the number of people provided with condoms and lubricant over time can still yield valuable insights into program implementation and progress in scaling up. 7. Baseline levels should first be measured before setting ambitious yet realistic targets and timeframes for scaling up comprehensive condom programming to reach a larger number and proportion of key populations. 8. These targets should consider logistical challenges and resources required to expand condom programming to key population-focused programs. 9. It is important to recognize that in nearly all countries, condoms and lubricants are also available for purchase from various outlets. 10. Distribution by key population-focused services, while critical for accessibility, does not represent the sole source contributing to overall condom coverage. 11. If lubricants are provided in tubes or containers instead of sachets, they should still be counted. 12. Condom-compatible lubricant should be provided with every condom distributed. If single-use sachets of lubricant are distributed, the target for this indicator should be a 1:1 ratio. 13. The percentage of key populations reporting they received lubricant when receiving condoms should be measured, with the target ideally set at 100%. 14. Needle and syringe programs (NSPs) should be accessible to people who inject drugs, including men who have sex with men, people in prisons, sex workers, and transgender individuals. 15. NSP sites should meet key population sensitization standards to ensure accessibility without stigma or discrimination. 16. The total number of sterile needles and syringes distributed by NSPs should be monitored to estimate the availability of clean injecting equipment in circulation. 17. For counting purposes, the total number of equivalent single sterile injecting units distributed should be calculated. For example, if 10 syringes and 20 needles are dispensed, this would count as 10 sterile injecting units. 18. Even if data on needles and syringes sold by pharmacies are unavailable, monitoring changes in the quantity of injecting equipment distributed over time can still provide valuable insights into program implementation and scaling up. 19. People who inject drugs require a continuous supply of injecting equipment, and limited quantities per visit may necessitate more frequent access to NSPs. 20. Baseline levels of needle-syringe distribution should be measured, and countries should set ambitious but realistic targets and timeframes for scaling up distribution relative to the estimated population size of people who inject drugs. 21. NSP sites may operate in various locations and service models, including fixed sites, mobile services, and outreach. For reporting purposes, a site must have frequent and regular hours of operation or access. 22. In some countries, injecting equipment may be available for purchase from pharmacies, while in others, access may be more restricted. 23. Behavioral surveys can be used to gather data on the percentage of people who report receiving sterile injecting equipment or condoms and lubricant within a specified time period. 24. The results of initial surveys can establish baselines for these indicators, and countries can then set targets and timeframes for achieving them, linked to program activities and scale-up efforts. 25. NSP utilization indicators examine service use relative to the estimated population size of people who inject drugs, with methods like unique identifier codes or recall last contact methods recommended to avoid double counting. 26. Regular access to NSPs, defined as at least once per month, is critical for ensuring a sufficient supply of clean injecting equipment and preventing the reuse of needles and syringes. 27. The total number of NSP client service events, including multiple visits by the same client, should be counted to assess service reach. 28. Targets for NSP coverage should be based on logistical assessments and resource requirements for scaling up capacity and implementing key population sensitization training and procedures. 29. The quantity of needles and syringes distributed per person who injects drugs per year can serve as a benchmark for evaluating program coverage and effectiveness. 30. Studies in developed countries and mathematical modeling suggest that higher levels of syringe distribution are required to prevent HIV and HCV transmission effectively.
